column4: The exact pair ٱلْءَاخِرَةَ وَٱلْأُولَىٰ is placed under divine ownership, supplying the closest Quranic frame for weighing the later and the first in 93:4.
Against a human being's wishes in 53:24, ٱلْءَاخِرَةُ وَٱلْأُولَىٰ both belong to God; the two times in the section are therefore gifts under one Owner.
The formula ٱلْءَاخِرَةُ خَيْرٌۭ وَأَبْقَىٰ repeats the section's judgment that the later is better and adds the reason that it lasts.
The same ayah joins a plea for postponement, أَخَّرْتَنَآ إِلَىٰٓ أَجَلٍۢ, to the answer that the afterlife is better, directly uniting the section's delay and comparison.
The statement that the afterlife is greater in degrees gives a second measure of the superiority expressed by خَيْرٌ in 93:4.
At resurrection the whole earlier stay seems no longer than an evening or its ضُحَىٰ, turning the section's unfinished morning interval into a measure of vanished first life.
Joseph identifies the present fulfillment as تَأْوِيلُ رُءْيَٰىَ مِن قَبْلُ; a word and vision from long before have reached the outcome meant by the section's dictionary sense of taʾwīl.
The wall's تَأْوِيل includes treasure kept hidden until two orphans mature, a concrete provision delayed yet secured until its proper time.
The prophetic address places what preceded and what came later, مَا تَقَدَّمَ ... وَمَا تَأَخَّرَ, immediately before God's completing His favor.
وَلَسَوْفَ يَرْضَىٰ matches both the emphatic future وَلَسَوْفَ and the promised satisfaction of 93:5, while naming the recipient differently.
One person meets a good promise while another has only been given present-life enjoyment; this is the section's secured later gift set directly against earlier possession.
Those who gave before the victory rank above those who gave afterward, yet God has promised both the best; temporal order, degrees, and assured good meet in one ayah.
لَهُ ٱلْحَمْدُ فِى ٱلْأُولَىٰ وَٱلْءَاخِرَةِ assigns both the first and later realm to God and ends with return to Him.
هُوَ ٱلْأَوَّلُ وَٱلْءَاخِرُ makes the First and the Last divine names, setting the section's relative human before and after inside an absolute boundary.
God knows both ٱلْمُسْتَقْدِمِينَ and ٱلْمُسْتَـْٔخِرِينَ, the precise opposition between advancing and coming later used to define الآخر in the section.
On the later Day each person is told what he sent ahead and left behind, بِمَا قَدَّمَ وَأَخَّرَ, so temporal placement becomes disclosed outcome.
At the cosmic ending every soul learns مَا قَدَّمَتْ وَأَخَّرَتْ, another exact joining of what was advanced and deferred with its final reckoning.
لِلَّهِ ٱلْأَمْرُ مِن قَبْلُ وَمِنۢ بَعْدُ gives God the before and after within the promised reversal from Roman defeat to victory.
ٱلْأَوَّلِينَ وَٱلْءَاخِرِينَ gathers earlier and later human generations into the single appointment specified by 56:50.
This ayah supplies the fixed endpoint for 56:49: both first and later peoples are assembled لَمَجْمُوعُونَ إِلَىٰ مِيقَـٰتِ يَوْمٍۢ مَّعْلُومٍۢ.
After commanding travel to see how creation began, the ayah says God produces ٱلنَّشْأَةَ ٱلْءَاخِرَةَ, the section's dictionary definition of the later abode as second creation.
ٱلنَّشْأَةَ ٱلْأُولَىٰ names the first creation and asks the hearer to infer the creation that follows it.
وَأَنَّ عَلَيْهِ ٱلنَّشْأَةَ ٱلْأُخْرَىٰ assigns the other or later creation to God, directly matching the section's lexical account of the afterlife.
As God began the first creation He will repeat it, and وَعْدًا عَلَيْنَآ إِنَّا كُنَّا فَـٰعِلِينَ makes that second beginning an expressly guaranteed promise.
The ayah combines universal return, وَعْدَ ٱللَّهِ حَقًّا, and God's beginning creation then repeating it, joining outcome, assurance, and second creation.
تُحِبُّونَ ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ identifies love of the immediate life as the preference whose other side is named in 75:21.
وَتَذَرُونَ ٱلْءَاخِرَةَ completes 75:20: the later is abandoned precisely because the immediate is preferred.
Those who love ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ leave behind a weighty future Day, a direct instance of choosing the nearer time over a consequential later one.
Preferring ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا states the mistaken choice to which 87:17 answers that the afterlife is better and more lasting.
وَلَلدَّارُ ٱلْءَاخِرَةُ خَيْرٌۭ names the later abode as better for the Godfearing, an exact repeated Quranic judgment behind 93:4.
وَٱلدَّارُ ٱلْءَاخِرَةُ خَيْرٌۭ contrasts the later home with people repeatedly taking the goods of the nearer world.
وَلَدَارُ ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ خَيْرٌۭ repeats the better-later formula after directing attention to the outcomes of former peoples.
The Godfearing answer that their Lord sent down good, and the ayah concludes that the home of the afterlife is better.
وَلَأَجْرُ ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ أَكْبَرُ describes later reward as greater, closely paralleling both خَيْرٌ in 93:4 and the greater degrees of 17:21.
The question أَرَضِيتُم بِٱلْحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا مِنَ ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ exposes satisfaction with the nearer life as a bad exchange because its enjoyment is little.
Those who prefer worldly life over the afterlife enact the very choice between first and later whose better term the section weighs.
They preferred worldly life over the afterlife, making explicit the human selection that reverses the section's scale.
ٱشْتَرَوُا۟ ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا بِٱلْءَاخِرَةِ turns the choice of the earlier life over the later into an actual transaction.
Those who sell worldly life for the afterlife are promised a great reward, joining the section's sale image to deferred divine payment.
God's purchase of believers' lives and wealth for Paradise is a covenant-backed transaction whose price is paid in the later abode.
Whoever wants the immediate is given a hastened allotment and then Hell; 17:19 supplies the opposite choice and 17:21 compares their degrees.
Whoever wants the afterlife and strives for it has effort gratefully accepted, the deferred counterpart to 17:18's hastened share.
كُلًّا نُّمِدُّ supplies both groups from the Lord's gift, preparing 17:21's comparison of how their outcomes differ.
The crop of the afterlife is increased, while one who wants the crop of this world receives some but no later share; the ayah makes temporal choice a harvest.
Pharaoh's magicians refuse to prefer him over the signs and observe that his power ends with this worldly life; 20:73 states what is better and lasting.
وَٱللَّهُ خَيْرٌۭ وَأَبْقَىٰ gives the converts' reason for accepting present punishment: God's forgiveness is better and more enduring.
Those who want worldly life and its adornment are paid their works in full here, setting the immediate payment whose later result appears in 11:16.
This ayah discloses the deferred outcome of 11:15's apparently complete worldly payment: they have nothing in the afterlife but the Fire.
The command to seek the later abode with what God has already given, without forgetting one's worldly share, holds the two times together without confusing their worth.
Whoever wants worldly reward is reminded that God possesses the reward of both this world and the afterlife, joining choice to the ownership stated in 92:13.
God gives from worldly reward to one who wants it and from afterlife reward to one who wants that, making two desired outcomes explicit alternatives.
God gives the believers worldly reward and the good reward of the afterlife, showing that an earlier gift can precede a better later one.
A petitioner asks only for this world and consequently has no share in the afterlife; 2:201 voices the fuller alternative.
The prayer asks for good both in this world and in the afterlife, placing the two goods together rather than treating the first as the whole gift.
Those who make the two-world prayer receive a share of what they earned, closing the choice staged by 2:200–201 with its outcome.
مَا عِندَكُمْ يَنفَدُ وَمَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ بَاقٍۢ distinguishes what runs out from what remains, explaining why a delayed divine good can be better.
ٱلْبَـٰقِيَـٰتُ ٱلصَّـٰلِحَـٰتُ are better with the Lord in reward and hope than the adornments named earlier in the ayah.
Enduring good deeds are better in reward and خَيْرٌۭ مَّرَدًّا, a better place of return that recalls the section's definition of taʾwīl as return and destination.
The transient bloom of worldly life is tested against وَرِزْقُ رَبِّكَ خَيْرٌۭ وَأَبْقَىٰ, the Lord's provision that is better and more lasting.
Worldly allotments are enjoyment and adornment, whereas what is with God is خَيْرٌۭ وَأَبْقَىٰ, giving the section's delayed promise its lasting scale.
What people are given is worldly enjoyment, while what is with God is better and more lasting for those who trust Him.
A crop pleases its growers, then dries and becomes debris, before the ayah names the later punishment or forgiveness; one visible season stages what passes and what awaits.
This worldly life is temporary enjoyment while the afterlife is دَارُ ٱلْقَرَارِ, the settled home, sharpening the contrast between passing first and abiding later.
The worldly life is play and diversion, while the later home is described as the true life, making second creation fuller life rather than mere continuation.
Every soul is told to look at what it has sent ahead لِغَدٍۢ, turning tomorrow into the reckoning date of today's investment.
Whatever good people send ahead they will find with God as better and greater in reward, a precise model of deferred value kept secure.
Whatever good is sent ahead is found with God later, so the apparent loss in the first time is preserved as the promised return.
The people of Paradise are told to eat and drink for what they sent ahead in past days, depicting the delayed payment at the moment it is received.
وَمَا نُؤَخِّرُهُۥٓ إِلَّا لِأَجَلٍۢ مَّعْدُودٍۢ says the coming Day is delayed only to a counted term, making postponement measured rather than uncertain.
The messengers offer forgiveness and postponement to an appointed term, joining a favorable grant to explicit temporal deferral.
God will forgive and postpone people to a named term, but the ayah also marks that the divine term cannot be postponed once it comes.
A prior word from the Lord and a specified term prevent immediate judgment, so an earlier divine commitment governs when the later event arrives.
A word that had already gone forth to an appointed term postpones judgment, another instance of delay resting on a prior divine determination.
Those who demand punishment be hastened are answered that God never breaks His promise, directly separating apparent delay from failed assurance.
When the revelation's تَأْوِيل comes, those who forgot it confess that the messengers brought truth; taʾwīl here is the long-deferred event reaching fulfillment.
They deny before knowledge encompasses it and وَلَمَّا يَأْتِهِمْ تَأْوِيلُهُۥ, so the eventual outcome has specifically not yet arrived.
Returning a dispute to God and the Messenger is called خَيْرٌۭ وَأَحْسَنُ تَأْوِيلًا, uniting what is better with what proves best in final outcome.
Honest measure is خَيْرٌۭ وَأَحْسَنُ تَأْوِيلًا; a transaction done rightly now is judged by its better eventual result.
سَأُنَبِّئُكَ بِتَأْوِيلِ promises a future explanation for what Moses could not await, and 18:82 supplies the wall's delayed-provision outcome.
God promises many future gains and says He has hastened this one, explicitly distinguishing an immediate installment from later promised gifts.
Another gain, not yet within the believers' power, is already encompassed by God; it closely matches fruit still on the branch yet secured.
Captives are told that if God knows good in them He will give something better than what was taken, making loss now the prelude to a promised better grant.
The child's parents are to receive from their Lord a replacement better in purity and mercy; this promised substitution is explained only after the painful earlier event.
سَيَجْعَلُ ٱللَّهُ بَعْدَ عُسْرٍۢ يُسْرًۭا makes ease a divinely promised later phase following present hardship.
With hardship comes ease, a promise that the present condition contains rather than cancels a better following condition.
The repeated assurance that ease accompanies hardship reinforces the certainty of the later good promised across 93:4–5.
The Gardens are promised while unseen, and إِنَّهُۥ كَانَ وَعْدُهُۥ مَأْتِيًّۭا says the promise is itself certain to arrive.
God makes the Messenger's vision come true and assures future safe entry into the Sacred Mosque, an old image reaching its appointed realization.
Help comes only after the messengers' wait reaches an extremity, making delayed rescue no evidence that the divine promise has disappeared.
The Romans' defeat is the first condition in the reversal whose promised later stages are stated in 30:3–6.
After their defeat, the Romans will prevail, staging a later condition that overturns the earlier one.
On the day of the promised reversal believers rejoice in God's help, naming the favorable outcome anticipated by 30:3–4.
وَعْدَ ٱللَّهِ لَا يُخْلِفُ ٱللَّهُ وَعْدَهُۥ seals the timed reversal of 30:2–5 as a promise that delay cannot invalidate.
The Messenger is told to be patient for what is promised; when people see it, their entire wait seems only an hour of a day.
At gathering, people feel they remained only an hour of the day, compressing the whole first interval once its outcome has arrived.
When the Hour rises, the guilty swear they stayed no more than an hour, another later vantage from which the earlier duration collapses.
The resurrection question asks how many years the people stayed on earth, opening the temporal reckoning answered in 23:113–114.
They answer that they stayed a day or part of one, voicing from the later life the felt brevity of the first.
The reply confirms that their stay was only little, had they known, completing the change of temporal scale begun in 23:112.
When God calls and people respond with praise, they suppose they had remained only a little, linking awakening and retrospective compression.
At resurrection people whisper that they stayed only ten days, a first estimate refined further in 20:104.
The most discerning say the stay was only one day, intensifying the later life's contraction of all that came before.
After being made to die for a hundred years, the man estimates a day or part of a day; restored life exposes the gulf between elapsed and perceived time.
Moses fixes the encounter as an appointed day and requires the people to gather ضُحًۭى, joining the section's morning threshold to a scheduled fulfillment.
The oath by the sun and ضُحَىٰهَا parallels 93:1's oath while making the brightening associated with that time explicit.
وَأَخْرَجَ ضُحَىٰهَا depicts God bringing out the sky's morning brightness, the growing-light feature developed in the section.
The Prophet is told to glorify before sunrise, before sunset, and at the day's ends so that he may be satisfied, joining ordered times to the hoped-for رِضَا.
Joseph tells people to sow for seven years and leave most grain in its ears, a harvest deliberately retained now for a later need.
Seven hard years will come after the years of sowing and consume the stored crop, making the deferred provision's purpose visible.
Then a year of rain and pressing arrives, completing the dream's timed sequence with relief after preservation and scarcity.
A debt contracted to a named term must be written down, the Quran's clearest scene of deferred payment made secure by a documented agreement.
A good loan to God is promised manifold repayment, using a present advance and guaranteed later increase as the section uses a deferred sale.
The one who lends God a good loan is promised multiplication and a noble reward, another contractual image for value held until later.
The grain that yields seven ears and manifold kernels makes delayed divine multiplication visible as a crop growing beyond the original gift.
Date palms and varied crops bear fruit, and their due is paid on harvest day; the ayah supplies the section's concrete endpoint of fruit and harvest.
Human life and revived earth unfold through successive stages toward a named term and resurrection, making a person's own first and later phases visible.
Creation proceeds from dust through infancy, maturity, and old age toward an appointed term, a full personal timeline on which earlier and later can be weighed.
The Lord creates and chooses, while creatures have no ٱلْخِيَرَةُ; this qualifies the section's dictionary sense of choosing the better of two things.
Once God and His Messenger decide a matter, believers have no خِيَرَةُ, setting a boundary on the human freedom implied by the choice sense of خير.
A disliked thing may be good and a loved thing bad because God knows the unseen outcome, showing why the better of two times cannot be judged from the first alone.
God promises one of two groups while the believers want the easier one, exposing a choice between alternatives whose truly good result God determines.
Postponing punishment to a counted period makes scoffers ask what holds it back; unlike the section's delayed gift, this secured later event is adverse.
God's apparent delay is not heedlessness: wrongdoers are postponed to a terrifying Day, reversing the section's favorable future while preserving its certainty.
People are postponed to a named term, but when it arrives they cannot delay or advance it even an hour; every granted interval has a hard boundary.
Human beings are deferred to an appointed term rather than seized immediately, making delay a respite before judgment rather than proof of a better outcome.
At death a person asks for postponement to a near term so he can give, showing the vain wish for one more credit period after its proper time has ended.
God will never postpone a soul once its term arrives, the explicit boundary to every image of payment or fruit carried forward.
When a community's term comes, it cannot be put back or brought forward by an hour, fixing the limit beyond which deferral is impossible.
No community can precede its appointed term or delay it, pairing temporal advance and postponement as an unalterable measure.
The Merciful extends the deluded until they see the threatened event; a longer first interval ends by exposing who has the worse station.
Unbelievers mistake granted time for good, but their respite only increases sin; this is the clearest reversal of the section's equation between later and better.
God grants respite while His plan remains firm, showing that an outcome can be fully secured even when delay favors the hearer only in appearance.
The garden owners swear they will harvest in the morning, staging an expected crop at a fixed later point whose security proves false.
A visitation circles the garden during the night while its owners sleep, interrupting the interval between their promise and 68:20's ruined morning.
By morning the garden is stripped dark, the opposite of the section's fruit remaining safely on its tree until harvest.
When the owners finally see the garden they first think they have lost the way, recording the moment expectation meets its altered outcome.
They recognize that they have been deprived, the failed harvest serving as a boundary case for the section's secured deferred gift.
A palm-and-vine garden is struck by a fiery whirlwind when its owner is old and vulnerable, reversing the image of fruit preserved safely to the end.
When the earth's growth ripens and its owners think it is under their power, God's command comes by night or daylight and leaves it harvested bare.
The garden owner assumes his wealth will never perish and that, if returned, he will find an even better resort; his claim mimics the better-later promise without divine warrant.
His fruit is encompassed and he wrings his hands over what he spent, showing a worldly crop whose expected future disappears.
After the garden's collapse, God's reward and outcome are declared better, distinguishing a true divine future from the owner's imagined one.
A person's later stage returns from strength to weakness and gray hair, showing that “later” alone does not lexically entail “better.”
Whomever God grants long life is reversed in creation, another personal later phase that qualifies any automatic equation of sequence with improvement.
The destruction of ٱلْأَوَّلِينَ gives the first generation an adverse end rather than a better continuation.
ثُمَّ نُتْبِعُهُمُ ٱلْءَاخِرِينَ makes the later generations follow the former in judgment, reversing 93:4's favorable relation between later and first.
The people of Paradise taste no death beyond the first death, so the first death becomes a boundary after which the later life no longer ends.
Joseph is promised instruction in taʾwīl and completion of favor near the beginning of his story; 12:100 later identifies the old dream's realized outcome.
تَأْوِيلِهِ can denote sought interpretation whose knowledge is contested or reserved to God; this semantic use cautions against reducing every taʾwīl to a visibly arrived event.
The sleepers estimate a day or part of one after awakening; 18:25's much longer count makes this a worldly analogue to resurrection's compressed first life.
The stated three hundred and nine years supply the objective duration that the sleepers of 18:19 experienced as only a day or less.
Divine punishment may arrive ضُحًۭى while a town plays, using the same daylight threshold as 93:1 but turning its growing light into exposed vulnerability.
The Prophet is told to be patient and glorify before sunrise and sunset, placing endurance of a delayed promise inside the ordered course of a day.
Night worship and glorification after prostrations continue the daily sequence begun in 50:39 beyond its two solar thresholds.
When a scribe is unavailable, a received pledge secures the obligation described in 2:282, making concrete the section's claim that deferred payment remains guaranteed.
The good tree gives its fruit at every appointed season by its Lord's permission, a Quranic image of fruit remaining ordered by divine timing.
The promised garden has enduring fruit and shade, carrying the section's harvest image into the later abode where provision no longer expires.
Believers are told not to count an apparent evil as evil for them but as good, a communal instance of the first appearance being corrected by its eventual value.
